sentences.text: One clinic has waited six episodes for its turn.
Elm: 11 patients, all lower-risk, and not one readmission. The best record in the cast.
So what is Elm's gamma? Ask the software, and it prints minus 6.25.
Ask again with its other fitting routine, and it prints minus 11.52.
Same patients. Same model. Two answers.
Which one is right? Neither. And seeing why shows us what to trust instead.
Welcome back to Model in Motion.
Today: no events, no peak.
Here is Elm's own hill: the height, for each position of its slider.
With the slider at the middle clinic's level, the height is minus 2.17. At minus 3, it is minus 0.53. At minus 6.25, minus 0.02.
It keeps rising, more and more slowly, toward a ceiling at zero that it never reaches.
A ramp, not a hill. There is no top to find.
The meter tells the same story. Elm observed no readmissions. But wherever the slider sits, the model expects more than none.
So expected always exceeds observed, and the meter always says: lower.
So the slider marches, about one unit a step, for as long as the fitting runs.
Stepping together stops once the dial has settled. That takes five steps, and leaves Elm's slider at minus 6.25.
Taking turns waits for every slider to settle, and Elm's never will.
So the software builds a wall, ten units below the middle clinic. Elm's slider runs into it and stops: minus 11.52.
Even the stopping rule matters. Loosen it, and stepping together prints minus 5.24. Tighten it: minus 7.25.
Each of these numbers records when an algorithm stopped. None of them is an estimate.
And nothing else is harmed. The dial and the other four sliders finish in the same place every time.
What breaks is anything built on that number.
Last episode's interval, from minus 19.7 to plus 7.2, was one casualty.
Here is a worse one. Suppose the reference is the average gamma, weighted by size.
That average is minus 1.75 after one routine, and minus 2.31 after the other.
Measured against it, Alder's readmissions come out at 1.87 times expected, or 2.76 times. Alder's patients did not change. Elm's stopping point did.
A clinic with no readmissions has quietly moved the yardstick for everyone.
What survives is anything built on the count.
Take the middle clinic as the reference instead. The median does not care how far out Elm's slider went: minus 1.52, either way.
At that reference, Elm's 11 patients would expect 1.97 readmissions. Elm had none.
How surprising is none? Each patient has an 82% chance of staying out. For all eleven, that comes to 11%.
Eleven percent is not rare. So Elm is not flagged. Zero is not automatically excellent.
But thirty such patients with no readmissions would be another matter: about three chances in a thousand.
The count speaks, even when gamma cannot.
Two footnotes. First, the mirror image: a clinic where every patient is readmitted runs to an upper wall instead.
Second, there was a sixth clinic. Fen, with 8 patients, never entered the fit, because the software screens out any provider with 10 records or fewer.
Elm, with 11, stayed in by a single patient.
Let's gather it up.
No readmissions means a hill with no top, and a printed gamma that only records where the fitting stopped.
Anything built on that gamma breaks. Anything built on the count survives.
And zero, from a handful of patients, is weak evidence.
That count, set against what the reference would expect, is the measure this whole series has been heading for.
Next time: swap the curve.
This has been Model in Motion. Thanks for following the story.
